k806: Durrës Yachts & Marina: reading the red flags of a Balkans megaproject
k807: This is the largest coastal development in the country — a joint venture between Eagle Hills and the Albanian state's ASDC agency, roughly 13,000 planned apartments and 280 yacht berths, publicly stated at €2–2.5 billion. It is also, in the KB's own words, the flagship case study for how to read a megaproject's red flags, and the facts are public and specific enough to be worth stating plainly rather than softened into a "some concerns have been raised" hedge.
k808: An independent geotechnical inspection (IKMT) confirmed subsidence of 28 cm and 18 cm in two completed buildings — the subcontractor on the project has separately claimed figures as high as 74 cm, a claim DomLivo treats as unconfirmed and flags accordingly. Sales began before full permits were issued. The financing model leans almost entirely on pre-sales rather than the investor's own capital — roughly 6.8% equity against a reported €42 million raised from buyers on a €7 million paid-in capital base. And the project's own timeline is tied to relocating the Porto Romano cargo port, a €410 million tender that has now failed twice, most recently in March 2026.
k809: None of that means the marina fails. It means a buyer here is exposed to construction-quality risk, a pre-sale structure without mandatory escrow, and a port-relocation dependency all at once — three separate ways for a purchase to go wrong, stacked in one project.

k835: How do you buy property in Albania in 2026?
k836: Buying in Albania is not complicated, but it is unforgiving about one thing: the contract has to be notarial. A private agreement between you and a seller, however carefully written, transfers nothing. It is void. People still sign them, usually because someone told them it was a deposit agreement, and the money is what gets lost.
k837: Everything below assumes you are buying as a foreign individual. That is the ordinary case and it carries no special restrictions.
k839: Reservation comes first, and it is where the money starts moving: 5–10% as <s1>kaparë</s1> on a resale, up to 30% on a new build. That deposit is the point of no comfortable return, so do the checking before it, not after.
k840: Due diligence takes one to two weeks and costs €500–2,000 for a lawyer. What they are pulling is the <s1>kartela e pasurisë</s1>, the encumbrance record, the <s3>harta treguese</s3>, and the title history. A lawyer is not required by law. Skipping one on a market where roughly 70% of civil cases concern land is a decision, not a saving.
k841: Then the preliminary contract, <s1>kontratë paraprake</s1> or <s3>premtim-shitje</s3>. For a new build this is the <s5>kontrata e porosisë</s5>, and since Udhëzim 1/2024 it must be notarial and registered in the ASHK register. This is the single change that killed the double-sale trick, where one unit went to several buyers on private paper.
k842: The notarial deed itself takes a day. Money moves through the notary's escrow account, and the notary withholds the taxes. If you do not speak Albanian, a Ministry of Justice sworn translator has to co-sign, which typically costs somewhere in the €50–150 range.
k843: Registration at ASHK is handled by the notary and you do not attend. The official term is 21 days. Realistically it is two to four weeks, and a complicated title can take months.

k859: Two notes on that table. The notary tariff is capped at about 150,000 lek and floored at 3,000, and if your contract price sits below the zone reference price, the tariff is calculated from the reference instead.
k860: On who formally pays the 2%: sources disagree. Portals say the buyer; the structure of the law points at a corporate transferor, with individual sellers paying 15% capital gains instead. In practice it is priced in, so argue about the total rather than the label. We would rather tell you the question is open than pick an answer.
k861: Older English-language guides quoting "€10–30" for cadastral fees are out of date. The current schedule runs 1,100 lek for a <s1>vërtetim pronësie</s1> up to 8,000 for a first registration.
k862: The eight things that actually go wrong
k863: Unregistered property is the big one. About 10% of the country never made it into the register, and the US State Department has flagged zones like Himara where up to 80% of the data carries errors. Check the <s1>kartela</s1> and the zone's first-registration status.
k864: Restitution claims from pre-1945 owners have been running since 1993 and are not finished. The coast is where they concentrate. Pull 30+ years of title history and check for claims sitting in ASHK or the courts.
k865: Legalised informal construction is subtler: the title exists, but if the former landowner was never compensated, the title can be challenged. Ask for the <s1>leje legalizimi</s1> and the compensation status of the plot.
k866: A building with no <s1>leje përdorimi</s1> cannot be properly registered, mortgaged or resold. Ask for the <s3>leje ndërtimi</s3>, the <s5>leje përdorimi</s5>, and confirmation the building itself is registered.
k867: A developer's <s1>hipoteka</s1> on the parent plot passes down to the units, so pull the encumbrance extract for the parent plot, not just your apartment. <s3>See how the Durrës Yachts & Marina project sits in this picture.</s3>
k868: Since Udhëzim 1557 of September 2024, ASHK compares the built layout against the approved plan and refuses registration where they diverge, with 30 days to fix it. This bites old contracts too. Walk the unit against the drawings before you pay.
k869: Boundary overlaps from poor mapping will block a transaction; a surveyor and the <s1>harta treguese</s1> settle it. And utility debt follows the meter, not the person, so get clearances from OSHEE, the water company and the building administrator.
k871: Slowly. First instance averages around 377 days and appeal around 2,272, according to the EU's 2025 Rule of Law report. Plan on avoiding court rather than winning in it.
